senses.def: a heavy object attached to a boat by a rope or chain and dropped to the bottom of a body of water in order to prevent or restrict the movement of the boat
senses.comment: For languages having no term for ‘anchor,’ one may use a descriptive equivalent, for example, ‘heavy weights on ropes to keep a boat from moving.’

senses.def: the space immediately above the earths surface, and not including the dome arching over the earth
senses.comment: The expression εἰς ἀέρα λαλοῦντες, literally ‘talking into the air,’ may be regarded as a type of idiom meaning ‘talking to no purpose’ or ‘talking without anyone understanding.’ Accordingly, ἔσεσθε γὰρ εἰς ἀέρα λαλοῦντες may be rendered as ‘you will be talking, but no one will understand’ or ‘you will be talking, but your words will not enter anyone.’ In Acts 22:23, κονιορτὸν βαλλόντων εἰς τὸν ἀέρα ‘throwing dust into the air,’ it may be more appropriate in a number of languages to say ‘throwing dust above themselves’ or simply ‘throwing dust up.’ A literal rendering of ‘throwing dust into the air’ might suggest in some languages that the air was some kind of a container in which the dust remained.|The Greek term ἀήρ in Revelation 9:2 (ἐσκοτώθη ὁ ἥλιος καὶ ὁ ἀὴρ ἐκ τοῦ καπνοῦ τοῦ φρέατος ‘the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the pit’) may very well be translated as ‘air,’ but since it is a reference primarily to space rather than to substance, it is more natural in a number of languages to say ‘the sky was darkened by the smoke from the pit.’

senses.def: air as an elemental substance
senses.comment: οὕτως πυκτεύω ὡς οὐκ ἀέρα δέρων ‘I do not box like someone hitting the air’ 1 Corinthians 9:26. In some languages it may be quite impossible to translate literally ‘hitting the air,’ for since the air is not regarded as a kind of material substance, it is impossible to hit it. The closest equivalent may be ‘hitting nothing’ or possibly ‘as though hitting something.’

senses.def: the space above the earth inhabited by and under the control of certain supernatural powers
senses.comment: In the context of Ephesians 2:2 ἐξουσία is best understood as a collective and thus referring to the various supernatural powers regarded as inhabiting the area above the earth and thus controlling in many respects both the behavior and the fate of people. See also 12.44.

senses.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
senses.comment: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.|In some instances a measure of meaning may be obtained by somewhat paraphrastic expressions. For example, Ephesians 2:2 is rendered in some languages as ‘at that time you lived in the way in which the spirit that governs this world dictated you should live. This is the way the one who rules over the power in space commanded you to live. This is the very spirit that now commands the people who disobey God.’

senses.def: pertaining to not producing seed, fruit, or harvest
senses.comment: In Jude 1:12 a literal rendering of ‘even in autumn’ might be misleading in some areas in which autumn as a calendrical term might not be the period for bearing fruit. Therefore, it might be better to translate Jude 1:12 as ‘trees that bear no fruit even in the season when they should.’

senses.def: pertaining to being useless, in the sense of being unproductive

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person belonging to a different socio-political group, with the implication of lack of kinship ties
(derivative of ἀναμιμνῄσκω ‘to cause to remember,’ 29.10) the means for causing someone to remember
to interrogate a defendant during a judicial hearing, often by means of torture or lashing
senses.comment: In the Roman legal system it was customary to use various forms of physical torture in order to extract confessions from persons who were not Romans and who had been charged with serious crimes, particularly crimes against the state.

senses.def: a martyr in Pergamum
a person greeted in Romans 16:10
to speak on behalf of oneself or of others against accusations presumed to be false
(derivative of ἀργός[a] ‘idle, not working,’ 42.46) to not be functioning
one who is a master or expert builder
to fix one’s eyes on some object continually and intensely
glosses: to keep one’s eyes fixed on
senses.comment: The expression ‘could not keep their eyes fixed on’ may be rendered as ‘could not keep looking at’ or ‘could not continue to look at.’

senses.def: to begin to sleep
senses.comment: It would obviously be a mistake to try to imitate the English idiom ‘to fall asleep,’ for this might be understood as ‘to go to sleep and as a result fall down’ or even ‘to fall down and then remain unconscious.’

senses.def: to speak much or extensively, with a possible added implication of meaningless words
glosses: to speak for a long time
senses.comment: For another interpretation of βατταλογέω in Matthew 6:7, see βατταλογέω[b] 33.89.

senses.def: to utter senseless sounds or to speak indistinctly and incoherently
senses.comment: For another interpretation of βατταλογέω in Matthew 6:7, see βατταλογέω[a] 33.88.|In some languages the equivalent of ‘to babble’ is ‘to speak like a baby’ or ‘to speak sounds that make no sense.’

senses.def: assistance in supplying what may be needed
(derivative of βοηθέω ‘to help,’ 35.1) an object which provides help or support
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be important to render βοήθεια[b] by something more specific, for example, 'ropes,´ as in 'they fastened some ropes tightly around the ship,´ since ropes may be the most likely reference in Acts 27:17.

senses.def: a renowned Pharisee in Jerusalem

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
senses.comment: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

senses.def: tenth in a series involving either time, space, or set
a tenth part of an object, series, or mass
senses.comment: In rendering ‘the tenth of the city fell’ in Revelation 11:13, it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘for every ten buildings, one building fell’ or ‘every tenth building in the city collapsed.’

senses.def: (semantic derivative of δέκατος[b] ‘tenth part,’ 60.65) a tenth of a substance being offered for some distinctive purpose
to refute completely in a debate
to cause the complete destruction of someone or something
senses.comment: In Revelation 11:18 there is a play on the two meanings of διαφθείρω. In the first instance the meaning is destroy, but in the second instance the meaning is ‘to deprave’ (see 88.266).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to become perverse or depraved, as a type of moral destruction
glosses: to cause the moral ruin of

senses.def: to become gradually incapacitated
to cut an object into two parts
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret διχοτομέω in Luke 12:46 as ‘severe punishment’ (see διχοτομέω[b], 38.12).

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of διχοτομέω[a] ‘to cut in two,’ 19.19) to punish with great severity
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand διχοτομέω in Matthew 24:51 and the parallel passage in Luke 12:46 in a strictly literal sense, namely, ‘to cut in two’ or ‘to cut into pieces’ (see 19.19).

senses.def: (derivative of δωρέομαι ‘to give,’ 57.83) pertaining to being freely given
pertaining to there being no cause or legitimate reason
pertaining to being without purpose
the worship of idols
pertaining to being astonished or alarmed
to cause to pour out
to scatter a substance or mass
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκχέω[a] ‘to pour out,’ 47.4) to cause to exist in an abundance
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκχέω[a] ‘to pour out,’ 47.4) to cause someone to experience something in an abundant or full manner

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: to flow out of a container
to give oneself over completely to some activity or state
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκχέω[e] ‘to flow out,’ 14.18) to be involved in experiencing something in an abundant manner
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκχέομαι ‘to pour out oneself,’ not occurring in the NT) to give oneself completely to some type of behavior
(an idiom, literally: to pour out blood) to cause the death of someone by violent means
senses.comment: The phrase πᾶν αἷμα δίκαιον ἐκχυννόμενον in Matthew 23:35 may be literally translated as ‘all innocent blood that is poured out.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the blood pours out) to die, with the implication of a sacrificial purpose
senses.comment: The relations between the various elements in this clause in Matthew 26:28 must in some instances be made somewhat more specific, for example, ‘by my dying, I am like a sacrifice for many for the purpose of their sins being forgiven.’ See also 23.107.

senses.def: a village in Judea, not far from Jerusalem

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to provide benefits, often with the implication of certain supernatural factors involved

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: to cause a duration to come to an end
to make someone completely adequate or sufficient for something
glosses: to cause to be fully qualified

senses.def: to assist in supplying what may be needed
to provide continuous and possibly prolonged assistance and help by supplying the needs of someone
to come to a conclusion in the process of thinking and thus to be in a position to make a decision
senses.comment: In some languages the process of ‘deciding’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to come to the end in one’s thinking’ or ‘to choose in one’s mind’ or ‘the mind sees its goal.’

senses.def: to allow someone to do something
a person who is associated with someone else, though not necessarily involving personal affection (as in the case of φίλος and φίλη, 34.11 and 34.12)
senses.comment: This meaning is also found as a variant reading: ὁμοία ἐστὶν παιδίοις καθημένοις ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς ἅ προσφωνοῦντα τοῖς ἑταίροις ‘like children sitting around in the marketplace and shouting to their companions’ Matthew 11:16 (apparatus; see Nestle-Aland).

senses.def: a state of beauty or fine appearance, with the implication of being attractive and well-suited

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: one who is deeply committed to something and therefore zealous

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a member of a Jewish nationalistic group seeking independence from Rome
senses.comment: It is possible that ζηλωτής in Luke 6:15 and Καναναῖος in Matthew 10:4 function not so much as a designation of an individual belonging to the particular Jewish nationalistic party (according to some scholars such a party may not have been organized at that time), but of one whjo is simply zealous for national independence (see ζηλωτής[a] ‘enthusiast, zealous person,’ 25.77). Therefore, one might speak of Simon as ‘Simon the patriot’ (the same applies to Acts 1:13, the only other occurrence of ζηλωτής[b] in the NT). To render ζηλωτής[b] as ‘armed insurrectionist’ or ‘guerilla fighter’ (as some translators have suggested) would be reading into the text more than is specifically warranted.

senses.def: a room for the storage of valuables
senses.comment: ταμεῖον[b] and θησαυρός[a] may often be rendered by descriptive phrases, for example, ‘a room where valuable things are kept’ or ‘a place where valuables are stored.’|In Matthew 12:35 θησαυρός[a] is used figuratively (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά ‘a good man draws good things from his good storehouse,’ meaning ‘… storehouse of good things’) to describe the heart as a kind of storehouse or treasure.

senses.def: a box in which money was kept
senses.comment: A ‘treasure box’ may be referred to as ‘a box with valuable objects’ or ‘a box with objects costing a great deal of money.’

senses.def: that which is of exceptional value and kept safe
(derivative of ἱερουργέω or ἱερατεύω ‘to serve as a priest,’ 53.85) one who performs religious rites and duties on behalf of others
to visit, with the purpose of obtaining information
senses.comment: In rendering ‘to get information from him’ it may be more satisfactory to say ‘to learn something from him’ or ‘to have him tell me what I needed to know.’

senses.def: the first son of Adam and Eve and the brother of Abel
to overburden someone by causing undue hardship
senses.comment: The meaning of ‘to cause undue hardship’ or ‘to overburden someone’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘to cause more trouble to someone than that person should have’ or ‘to cause more suffering than what is right.’

senses.def: to consider something of a comparable merit or worth
glosses: to regard as being valuable for

senses.def: (derivative of κατηγορέω ‘to accuse,’ 33.427) one who brings accusation
to announce in a formal or official manner by means of a herald or one who functions as a herald
to announce extensively and publicly
to publicly announce religious truths and principles while urging acceptance and compliance
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate κηρύσσω[c] without indicating the content of what is preached. Accordingly, one may have such expressions as to preach about the good news or to preach about God.

senses.def: a room in a house for sleeping
senses.comment: It would be wrong to render the expression ‘who was in charge of the king’s bedroom’ in Acts 12:20 as meaning simply one who kept the bedroom clean. A person such as Blastus would have been a highly respected person with considerable responsibility for the king’s living quarters and personal affairs. The expression may be adequately rendered in Acts 12:20 by speaking of Blastus as ‘a high official.’

senses.def: to cause to hang down from
(an idiom, literally: to hang on a tree) to execute someone by nailing that person to a cross
senses.comment: It is possible to understand ξύλου in Acts 5:30 as ξύλον[f] ‘cross’ (6.28) and to interpret the expression literally as ‘… you seized and killed by hanging him on a cross.’

senses.def: to hang down from some point
to be in a relation of dependency upon something
senses.comment: In a number of languages dependency as in Matthew 22:40 may be expressed as ‘to hang on’ or ‘to be tied together by’ or ‘only have meaning because of.’

senses.def: an island in the Aegean Sea
a district in north Africa
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause to move from one place to another by bringing or leading
(derivative of μιμέομαι ‘to imitate,’ 41.44) one who imitates someone else
glosses: one who does what others do

senses.def: that which constitutes a defect or blemish, either in the physical or moral sense
senses.comment: The context of 2 Peter 2:13 is highly figurative, and the occurrence of μῶμος may be regarded as an instance of figurative usage.

senses.def: a city on the west coast of Greece
a general term for a thoroughfare, either within a population center or between two such centers
to be in the process of travelling, presumably for some distance
senses.comment: Note that ὁδός[b] may also refer to a particular journey, as in Luke 2:44, ἦλθον ἡμέρας ὁδόν ‘they made a day’s trip.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὁδός[a] ‘road,’ 1.99) a customary manner of life or behavior, with probably some implication of goal or purpose
(a figurative extension of meaning of ὁδός[a] ‘road, way,’ 1.99) behavior in accordance with Christian principles and practices
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to preserve the figurative meaning of ὁδός in Acts 9:2, and therefore it may be necessary to translate the first part of Acts 9:2 simply as ‘so that if he could find any who were followers of Christ’ or ‘… those who were Christians.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: a straight road) the right or correct pattern of behavior
(an idiom, literally: to prepare the road) to cause circumstances to be ready or propitious for some event
senses.comment: In some languages it may be better to render this expression in Matthew 11:10 as ‘who will arrange everything for you.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: a Sabbath’s road) a Sabbath day’s journey, somewhat over half a mile and about one kilometer
pertaining to conforming closely to an accepted norm or standard

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: eye, normally including the eyelids
senses.comment: In a number of languages an important distinction is made between the eyes consisting of the eyeballs and the eyes covered or partially covered by the eyelids. In Matthew 9:29 and Matthew 20:34, Jesus apparently touched the eyelids, not the eyeballs.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὀφθαλμός[a] ‘eye,’ 8.23) the capacity to see
(a figurative extension of meaning of ὀφθαλμός[a] ‘eye,’ 8.23) capacity to understand as the result of perception
senses.comment: In both Luke 19:42 and Ephesians 1:18 ὀφθαλμός designates a faculty of understanding and is not a reference merely to perception. In Ephesians 1:18 καρδία denotes the mind (see 26.3), so that the phrase ‘the eyes of the mind’ really means ‘the capacity for understanding which the mind has.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: evil eye) a feeling of jealousy and resentment because of what someone else has or does
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός in Matthew 20:15 as meaning ‘stinginess’ (see 57.108). See also 23.149.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: evil eye) to be stingy
senses.comment: It is also possible that ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός in Matthew 20:15 is to be understood in the sense of ‘jealous’ (see 88.165). See also 23.149.

senses.def: (idioms, literally: their eyes were weighed down) to become excessively or exceedingly sleepy
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ἦσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ βεβαρημένοι (or καταβαρυνόμενοι) would be ‘they could no longer keep their eyes open’ or ‘they could not drive sleep away.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to close the eyes) to be unwilling to learn and to evaluate something fairly
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a problem involved in a literal rendering of ‘to close the eyes,’ since this may be understood in a strictly literal sense or as denoting death.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to blind the eyes) to cause someone to no longer have the capacity for understanding
senses.comment: Though in some languages there is a close relationship between the eyes and comprehension, in many languages it is simply impossible to use the idiom ‘to blind the eyes’ in speaking of ‘causing someone not to understand.’ The problem becomes particularly difficult in speaking of ‘darkness blinding the eyes’ as in 1 John 2:11. People can understand how ‘bright light would blind the eyes,’ but it would be strange indeed to think of ‘darkness’ having such an effect. In the context of 1 John 2:11, the darkness is, of course, not literal darkness but a state of sinfulness. Therefore, in some languages it may be necessary to translate ‘their sinfulness has made it impossible for them to understand’ or ‘because they sin, they cannot understand.’

senses.def: to continue to move along

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move past a reference point
to go out of existence
pertaining to joining with someone under false pretenses and motivations
senses.comment: It is possible that παρείσακτος in Galatians 2:4 may be interpreted as a passive in the sense of ‘induced to join.’

senses.def: to convince someone to believe something and to act on the basis of what is recommended
to believe in something or someone to the extent of placing reliance or trust in or on
senses.comment: In a number of languages trust or reliance is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to lean one’s weight on’ or ‘to hang upon’ or ‘to place oneself in the hands of.’

senses.def: to submit to authority or reason by obeying
to be a disciple or follower of someone, in the sense of having put one’s confidence in a leader
to come to believe the certainty of something on the basis of being convinced
(an idiom, literally: to convince the heart) to exhibit confidence and assurance in a situation which might otherwise cause dismay or fear
to move to and strike against, involving both movement and impact
senses.comment: Since the context of Acts 27:41 involves a ship, it is important to select terms which will be appropriate for such an event.

senses.def: to become subject to physical control, with the implication of harmful consequences
glosses: to fall into the hands of
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be more appropriate to use what may be called ‘an active form,’ for example, ‘robbers seized him.’

senses.def: to experience somewhat suddenly that which is difficult or bad

senses.subdomain: Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of πλανάω ‘to cause to wander off the path,’ not occurring in the NT) act of causing someone to hold a wrong view and thus be mistaken
senses.comment: To mislead people as to proper views which they should have may often be expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to twist people’s thoughts,’ ‘to cause what is false to seem like what is true,’ ‘to make a lie appear true,’ ‘to dig away the truth,’ or ‘to cover the eyes with lies.’

senses.subdomain: Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
senses.def: (semantic derivative of πλάνη[a] ‘deception,’ 31.8) the content of that which misleads or deceives

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: behavior which deviates seriously from that which is morally correct
senses.comment: In a number of languages πλάνη in Romans 1:27 may be rendered as ‘what people do which is completely wrong’ or ‘… what is very wrong indeed.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the right to be a citizen of a particular socio-political entity (see 11.67 and 11.68)
senses.comment: In some languages Acts 22:28 may be rendered as ‘I obtained the right to be counted as a citizen’ or ‘I became a person who belongs to that nation.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a group of people constituting a socio-political unit
senses.comment: It is possible that in Ephesians 2:12 the use of πολιτεία suggests not merely a socio-political but also a socio-religious grouping. Such a conclusion would, in a sense, be true of any and all designations of a Jewish constituency, since religion and ethnic identification were so inextricably bound together.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: gentleness of attitude and behavior, in contrast with harshness in one’s dealings with others
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘gentleness’ is often expressed as a negation of harshness, so that ‘gentleness’ may often by rendered as ‘not being harsh with people,’ but gentleness may also be expressed in some instances in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘always speaking softly to’ or ‘not raising one’s voice.’

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to think about something ahead of time, with the implication that one can then respond appropriately
glosses: to have in mind to do

senses.def: to care for or look after, with the implication of continuous responsibility
to imitate a particular type of behavior as a means of indicating a presumed intent
(a figurative extension of meaning of πτῶσις ‘fall,’ not occurring in the NT) to suffer destruction or ruin, with the implication of having formerly held a position of eminence
senses.comment: In rendering εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν in Luke 2:34 it is important to indicate clearly that some are to be destroyed and others are to rise. If one translates literally ‘for the destruction and rise of many,’ it might imply that certain individuals are to be destroyed and then to rise again. For other interpretations of this passage, see 13.59 and 87.75.

senses.subdomain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πτῶσις ‘fall,’ not occurring in the NT) radical change toward a lower status (note the contrast with ἀνάστασις[b] rising up, 87.39)
senses.comment: For somewhat different interpretations of πτῶσις in Luke 2:34, see 20.50 and 13.59.

senses.def: to change for the worse, with emphasis upon extent and suddenness
senses.comment: For somewhat different interpretations of πτῶσις in Luke 2:34, see 20.50 and 87.75.

senses.def: to be forcibly tossed back and forth
pertaining to what is human or characteristic of human nature
pertaining to being material or physical, with the possible implication of inferior
senses.comment: It is possible that σαρκικός in Romans 15:27 refers to blessings for the body, but the context would seem to imply blessings of greater significance than those designed only for a person’s body.

senses.def: pertaining to the natural, physical characteristics of persons and often including their characteristic behavior
(derivative of σάρξ[f] ‘human nature,’ 26.7) pertaining to behavior which is typical of human nature, but with special focus upon more base physical desires
senses.comment: In some languages the expression τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν in 1 Peter 2:11 may be rendered as ‘the desires which one’s body has’ or ‘what the body wants.’

senses.def: Mount Zion, a hill within the city of Jerusalem
the city of Jerusalem together with its people, particularly in poetic discourse; see also 11.66
to scatter seed over tilled ground
senses.comment: In many languages there is a problem of translating σπείρω literally as ‘to scatter seed,’ since this is interpreted as an exceedingly wasteful manner of sowing, but unless one translates more or less literally and then provides some explanatory footnote, the parable loses much of its significance for many cultures.

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.comment: In some languages a distinction is made between terms used for the mouth when it is open and when it is closed. In Acts 23:2 presumably the mouth was closed.|The term στόμα also occurs in a number of phrases associated with speech, but while in some languages one can say ‘to speak with the mouth,’ it may be more appropriate to say ‘to speak with the lips’ or ‘to speak with the tongue.’ In a number of contexts, however, it may be better simply to say ‘to speak,’ since the addition of ‘with the lips’ or ‘with the tongue’ or ‘with the mouth’ may appear to be unnecessarily redundant.

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of στόμα[a] ‘mouth,’ 8.19) to communicate orally
(figurative extension of meaning of στόμα[a] ‘mouth,’ 8.19) the faculty or capacity for speech
senses.comment: In Luke 1:64 στόμα and γλῶσσα[e] appear to have the same referent and therefore may be regarded as essentially synonymous.

senses.def: that which has been spoken or uttered
(a figurative extension of meaning of στόμα[a] ‘mouth,’ 8.19) the sharp edge of a weapon
senses.comment: For a discussion of στόμα μαχαίρης, see 6.33.

senses.subdomain: In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: mouth to mouth) the position of persons facing one another and engaged in discussion
(an idiom, literally: to open the mouth to) to speak the complete truth to someone
glosses: to speak the whole truth to

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to block the mouth) to cause someone not to have anything to say
glosses: to remove any reason to speak

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to shut the mouth) to prevent harm or injury being done (in the one context in the NT, Hebrews 11:33, a reference to lions)
senses.comment: The particular historical reference of this phrase in Hebrews 11:33 is not clear. In the account in it is the angel of God which shut the mouths of the lions.

senses.def: to take by force that which belongs to someone else (often used of taking spoils of war, but occurring in the NT only figuratively of Pauls accepting financial support from some churches in order to help others)
to experience restorative rest together with someone else (see ἀναπαύομαι[a] ‘to rest,’ 23.80)
glosses: to rest together with someone else

senses.def: to come near to or to reach, with the implication of some type of association
hardship resulting in wretchedness
senses.comment: ‘Wretchedness’ may be expressed idiomatically in some languages as ‘to have nothing’ or ‘to have even one’s shirt in rags.’

pertaining to receptors
to be left behind, with the implication of continuing to exist
light, in contrast with darkness (σκότος[a], σκοτία[a], 14.53), usually in relationship to some source of light such as the sun, moon, fire, lamp, etc.
senses.comment: Terms for ‘light’ often differ on the basis of whether there is a specific source of light, for example, a fire, lamps, sun, moon, etc., or whether the light is simply generalized, in the sense of daylight apart from the actual shining of the sun (for example, as in the interior of a room). Some languages also make distinctions between terms for light depending on whether the light comes from a fire or lamp or from a heavenly body.|In a number of languages there is no noun for ‘light,’ but only verbs are employed, since the fact of light is spoken of as something which happens and is hence regarded as an event.

senses.def: flowering plant species in the palm family Arecaceae; grows to 10-20 m tall; cluster of large leaves at top; Phoenix dactylifera; cultivated for its edible sweet fruit, about the size of a human thumb; symbol of elegance and grace; palm branch is symbol of peace and also victory
senses.comment: See discussion at 3.53.

senses.def: branch of the palm tree (φοῖνιξ)
senses.comment: βάϊον is a technical term meaning ‘palm branch,’ and in John 12:13 τῶν φοινίκων ‘of palm trees’ may have been added redundantly, since the term βάϊον may not have been regarded as sufficiently well known to readers.|In the contexts in which φοῖνιξ[a] (John 12:13; see 3.8) and φοῖνιξ[b] (Revelation 7:9) occur in the NT, it is important to obtain a satisfactory term for branch, since in a number of languages a very important distinction is made between branches of palm trees, which are often called leaves (technically they are), and branches of most other trees (often spoken of idiomatically as arms of the trees).

to make known a divine revelation
glosses: to reveal a message from God

senses.def: to give a name or title to
a position relatively near the speaker, writer, or viewpoint person
senses.comment: Though ὧδε[a] and ἐνθάδε may seem to be rendered in some contexts as to here or hither, the semantic component of movement is not found in ὧδε[a] or ἐνθάδε, but in other words in the context indicating movement.
